implementation_notes: The classic roles collapse into data plus a loop: the recipient set is a std::vector of endpoints - a socket or queue handle, or a std::function<void(const Message&)> target - computed per message, and the traversal is a range-for that hands each element its own copy. std::function (or a variant of concrete targets) supplies the polymorphism that a Router class hierarchy used to provide, so no new type is needed until per-recipient policy becomes pluggable. The class-based classic form is still justified when handlers must be configured and swapped independently of the router, or when a framework (ACE, Asio) already owns the event loop and expects hand-off objects.
pitfalls: Passing the message by const& is only safe while deliver() does not retain it; if a recipient stores a reference, all recipients share mutable state and content changes leak across the fan-out.
A std::function target capturing a reference to a short-lived connection or buffer dangles once the loop moves on; the recipient container must own what its targets use.
Sequential delivery makes total latency the sum of all sends, so one slow or dead endpoint delays every later recipient unless sends are made asynchronous or time-bounded.

variants.name: Boost.Asio asynchronous fan-out with a completion barrier
variants.idiom_name: asio::async_write per recipient + pending counter / make_parallel_group
variants.implementation_notes: The recipient set becomes a vector of connected sockets or Asio objects and the traversal becomes N async_write operations started from one loop; a shared pending counter (or boost::asio::experimental::make_parallel_group, which Asio provides for exactly this co-ordination) fires the completion when the last recipient has been written to. This variant replaces the blocking loop's latency summation with true overlap while keeping one thread; the manual loop remains the better choice for few, local or genuinely blocking destinations.
pitfalls: The payload buffer, the sockets and the completion handler state must outlive every outstanding async_write; dangling buffers are the classic Asio fan-out bug.
Without a per-send timeout or cancellation, a dead peer leaves the pending counter above zero and the completion never fires - Asio cancellation slots/steady_timer are the tools.

variants.name: Boost.Asio fan-out with C++20 coroutines
variants.implementation_notes: Stackless coroutines turn the fan-out back into a linear loop over the computed recipient list: each co_await async_write delivers one copy, and because the loop body is sequential the completion condition is just the loop ending. Use it when the toolchain is C++20 and readability of the per-recipient error handling matters; the callback variant still wins when all sends must overlap, and co_spawn with awaitable_operators (&&/||) covers that case without leaving the coroutine model.
pitfalls: A coroutine loop is sequential by construction: total latency is the sum of the sends, so overlap requires co_spawn plus awaitable_operators instead.
Awaited operations throw a system_error by default; without as_tuple/redirect_error one failed recipient aborts the fan-out mid-list.
